note: Phase 2 priority sources plus democracy, justice/safety, assistance, Popular Sovereignty, Energy Sovereignty EIA/DOE structural baselines, Health/CMS/HRSA/CDC/ACHI structural baselines, Prosperous Aging SSA/GAO/IRS baselines, Family Farm USDA ERS/FNS baselines, Community Prosperity ICI/MSRB baselines, Community Resilience ISO/NFPA baselines, and Local Ownership NCEO/USDA baselines. No fabricated findings. Secondary sources labeled. Phase 2.1 continuation (2026-08-07): added CC-SRC-081–090 for first-20 claim audit (monopsony, corporate-tax incidence, e-commerce, Wayfair, NSF R&D, property-tax relief, productivity measurement dispute).

sources.title: Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2019 to 2022: Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances
authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
sources.summary: Triennial SCF results: real median net worth rose 37% to $192,900 (2022); real mean net worth rose 23% to $1,063,700. Patterns imply some narrowing of the wealth distribution between 2019 and 2022 while levels remain highly unequal (mean far above median).
key_findings: Median net worth $192,900 in 2022 (2022 dollars)
Mean net worth $1,063,700 in 2022
Largest three-year median net-worth increase in modern SCF history
sources.limitations: Survey-based; top-coded extremes; snapshot years; does not by itself establish causes of concentration.
sources.notes: Preferred primary source for household balance-sheet levels.

sources.title: Distributional Financial Accounts — Distribution of Household Wealth in the U.S. since 1989
authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
sources.summary: Quarterly Distributional Financial Accounts integrate SCF microdata with Financial Accounts aggregates. Wealth remains highly concentrated; bottom half of the wealth distribution holds a small share of total wealth.
key_findings: FRED DFA share tables (Q1 2026): top 1% ≈ 28.8% of wealth; 90th–99th ≈ 34.7%; bottom 50% ≈ 5.3%
Implies top decile near ~63.5% of household wealth in that quarter
sources.limitations: Model-based quarterly estimates; methodology differs from SCF point estimates; shares vary by quarter and asset definition.
sources.notes: Use for concentration shares; cross-check with SCF for levels.

sources.title: Understanding the labor productivity and compensation gap
sources.summary: BLS Beyond the Numbers analysis: productivity and compensation rose together for decades after the 1940s, then diverged since the 1970s at aggregate and many industry levels.
key_findings: Documents a productivity–compensation gap since the 1970s
Industry detail shows compensation lagging productivity in most studied industries (1987–2015)
sources.limitations: Measurement choices (deflators, sectors, compensation vs typical-worker pay) affect gap size; article is older than current BLS releases.
sources.notes: Primary federal acknowledgment of divergence phenomenon.

sources.title: The Productivity–Pay Gap
sources.summary: EPI constructs a net-productivity vs typical-worker hourly compensation series from BLS and BEA inputs. Reports large cumulative divergence since 1979 (e.g., net productivity up far more than typical-worker pay).
key_findings: From 1979 to 2020, EPI reports net productivity +61.8% vs typical-worker hourly pay +17.5% (inflation-adjusted), per their methodology page
sources.limitations: Advocacy-affiliated research institute; series construction choices (typical worker definition, net productivity) are contested; not a federal official series.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Progressive labor-oriented think tank — use alongside BLS primary series, not alone.
sources.notes: Secondary synthesis; preserve as one perspective on the gap.

sources.title: Economic Census 2022 — Concentration of Largest Firms (EC2200SIZECONCEN)
sources.summary: Official Economic Census establishment/firm-size concentration ratios (CR4/CR8/CR20/CR50 and related measures) for U.S. industries.
key_findings: Provides industry-level concentration ratios for 2022 Economic Census
Enables tracking of largest-firm shares of sales/shipments/revenue
sources.limitations: Industry definitions and national aggregation; concentration ≠ proven market power; not a single economy-wide monopoly index.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Official Census Bureau Economic Census product.
sources.notes: Primary source for competition domain architecture.

sources.title: Does employee ownership improve performance?
sources.summary: IZA World of Labor synthesis: over 100 studies generally link employee ownership to better productivity, pay, job stability, and survival on average; effects are dispersed and causation is difficult to establish firmly. Meta-analysis finds small positive average performance association.
key_findings: Small but significant average positive association with firm performance in meta-analysis (r̄≈0.04 cited)
Free-rider problems may be mitigated by complementary workplace practices
sources.limitations: Selection into ESOPs; heterogeneous designs; publication bias risk; not proof that all ownership forms always improve outcomes.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Academic synthesis; author is a leading EO researcher.
sources.notes: Supports 'can improve' not 'always improves'.

sources.title: Research findings on employee ownership
sources.summary: NCEO research digest summarizing studies associating ESOPs with productivity, retention, and crisis resilience in some samples, including food-industry COVID comparisons.
key_findings: Cites meta-analysis of 102 studies with small positive performance link
Reports ESOP adoption associated with labor-productivity increases in some establishment studies
sources.limitations: Advocacy/membership organization for employee ownership; selection effects; results vary by governance quality.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Pro-employee-ownership nonprofit — pair with independent academic reviews.
sources.notes: Secondary; opposing caveat is selection and small average effects.

sources.title: Rural America at a Glance, 2025 Edition
sources.summary: ERS annual nonmetro overview: ~46.2 million nonmetro residents (13.6% of U.S.) in July 2024; nonmetro growth slower than metro; 51% of nonmetro counties declined 2020–2024 despite aggregate nonmetro gains from migration.
key_findings: Nonmetro population 46.2 million (July 2024), 13.6% of U.S.
51% of nonmetro counties lost population July 2020–June 2024
sources.limitations: County typology and metro adjacency matter; aggregate nonmetro gains mask widespread county decline.
sources.notes: Primary rural demography source.

sources.title: 146 rural hospitals closed or stopped providing inpatient services from 2005 to 2023
sources.summary: ERS chart note: 146 rural-county hospitals closed or converted from acute inpatient care (2005–2023); 81 shut down completely; financial stress is primary driver.
key_findings: 146 closures/conversions 2005–2023
81 complete shutdowns
sources.limitations: Does not measure access minutes for all communities; conversion still leaves some services.
sources.notes: Healthcare access proxy for rural resilience.

sources.title: Long-Term Trends in Rural Depopulation and Their Implications for Community Banks
sources.summary: FDIC analysis: more than half of rural counties lost population 1980–2010; community bank charters in depopulating rural areas declined sharply with industry consolidation.
key_findings: Over half of rural counties lost population 1980–2010
Community bank charters in depopulating rural areas fell substantially 1984–2012
sources.limitations: Older article; banking structure has continued to change; does not prove causation from depopulation alone.
sources.notes: Historical structural context for local capital access.

sources.title: Earnings, Income, and Wealth Inequality in America: New Evidence from the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances (NBER WP 33823)
sources.summary: NBER working paper on 2022 SCF: wealth remains highly concentrated; reports top 1% holding about 35% of wealth in 2022, down from a 2016 peak near 39%, with housing gains benefiting middle-class households.
key_findings: Top 1% wealth share ≈35% in 2022 SCF analysis (paper)
Concentration declined modestly from mid-2010s peak while remaining high
sources.limitations: Working paper (not peer-reviewed final); estimates depend on SCF processing choices; differs from DFA quarterly shares.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Academic working paper — secondary to Fed SCF bulletin.
sources.notes: Use as secondary corroboration; prefer Fed SCF/DFA for official citation.

sources.title: FRED — Shares of Wealth by Wealth Percentile Groups (Distributional Financial Accounts)
authors: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis / Board of Governors
sources.summary: FRED release tables for DFA wealth shares by percentile groups.
sources.limitations: Quarterly model-based shares; subject to revision.
sources.notes: Canonical share figures for baseline metrics.

sources.title: The Distribution of Household Income in 2021
sources.summary: CBO distributional analysis of household income, means-tested transfers, and federal taxes for 2021. Highest-quintile average income before transfers/taxes roughly 19× lowest quintile; after transfers and taxes about 7×. Federal taxes and transfers reduce measured inequality but do not eliminate concentration of income and tax payments at the top.
key_findings: Highest-quintile average income before transfers/taxes ≈19× lowest quintile in 2021
After transfers and taxes, highest/lowest ratio ≈7×
Pandemic-era transfers and credits raised lower-income incomes while capital gains raised top incomes
sources.limitations: CBO income/tax concepts differ from IRS AGI or SCF wealth; 2021 includes temporary pandemic policies; incidence assumptions are model-based.
sources.notes: Primary federal source for income/tax distribution architecture.

sources.title: Rucho v. Common Cause, 588 U.S. ___ (2019)
authors: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.summary: Holding: partisan-gerrymandering claims present political questions beyond the reach of federal courts. Leaves substantial reform pathways to Congress, state constitutions and courts, commissions, and voters.
key_findings: Partisan gerrymandering claims held nonjusticiable in federal courts as political questions
Does not authorize partisan gerrymandering; channels remedies largely outside federal judicial policing of partisan maps
sources.limitations: Legal holding, not an empirical map-fairness study; state and congressional avenues remain; racial vote-dilution doctrines are distinct.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: U.S. Supreme Court majority opinion; dissent exists and should be read for contrary constitutional theory.
sources.notes: Primary legal context for redistricting reform architecture.

sources.title: Redistricting Commissions: State Legislative Plans
sources.summary: NCSL overview of state redistricting commission and related nonlegislative arrangements for state legislative plans; structures and independence vary by state.
key_findings: Multiple states use commissions or other nonlegislative arrangements
Commission design and independence are not uniform
sources.limitations: Secondary institutional summary; verify against state constitutions/statutes for any specific state claim.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Bipartisan state legislative association research/service organization.
sources.notes: Use for institutional variation; not a single national commission mandate.

sources.title: Legislative Term Limits: An Overview
sources.summary: NCSL overview of state legislative term limits. A minority of states use them; literature and experience include both rotation-of-power aims and concerns that influence can shift toward lobbyists, staff, agencies, and party organizations when legislative institutional knowledge declines.
key_findings: Sixteen states currently have legislative term limits (per NCSL overview context)
Term limits are not a complete anti-capture solution
sources.limitations: Secondary overview; effects vary by state design; count and details should be re-checked against current NCSL tables before publication of exact tallies.
sources.notes: Supports caution against treating term limits as sufficient officeholder-integrity design.

sources.title: Community Policing Defined
authors: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Community Oriented Policing Services (COPS Office)
sources.summary: Defines community policing as organizational strategies supporting partnerships and problem-solving to address conditions that give rise to crime, social disorder, and fear of crime. Identifies three key components: Community Partnerships, Organizational Transformation, and Problem Solving.
key_findings: Community policing comprises Community Partnerships, Organizational Transformation, and Problem Solving
Police rarely can solve public safety problems alone; interactive partnerships with stakeholders are central
sources.limitations: Philosophical/operational definition document, not an outcome evaluation of a specific local Community Safety Corps design.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: DOJ COPS Office publication defining federal community-policing vocabulary.
sources.notes: Foundation for carrying community-policing elements further into a complete Community Safety Corps architecture.

sources.title: Phasing Out Our Use of Private Prisons
authors: Sally Q. Yates, Deputy Attorney General (U.S. Department of Justice)
sources.summary: DOJ announcement accompanying the August 18, 2016 Yates memorandum directing the Bureau of Prisons to reduce and ultimately end the use of privately operated prisons, citing concerns including safety and correctional services compared with BOP facilities.
key_findings: 2016 DOJ directive sought to reduce and phase out privately operated federal prisons
Rationale cited comparative concerns about privately operated facilities
sources.limitations: Federal BOP contracting posture only; does not itself settle state/local private-jail or private-probation rules; later rescinded (see CC-SRC-019).
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Obama-administration DOJ policy; superseded by later administrations.
sources.notes: Use with CC-SRC-019 to document private-prison policy instability across administrations — not as an invented national privatization prevalence statistic.

sources.title: Memorandum: Rescission of Memorandum on Use of Private Prisons
authors: Jefferson B. Sessions III, Attorney General (U.S. Department of Justice)
sources.summary: February 21, 2017 Attorney General memorandum rescinding the August 18, 2016 Yates memorandum and directing that the Department will continue to use private prisons as needed.
key_findings: 2017 Sessions memorandum rescinded the 2016 Yates private-prison phase-down directive
Illustrates that federal private-prison contracting policy can reverse across administrations
sources.limitations: Federal BOP policy only; later executive orders and contracting decisions may further change posture; does not quantify state/local private corrections markets.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Trump-administration DOJ policy reversing prior directive.
sources.notes: Corrects informal claims that a 2023 memorandum was the rescission; the documented rescission of the Yates memo is the 2017 Sessions memo. Later EO/policy churn reinforces the case for settling principle in law.

sources.title: Adult Treatment Court Program | Overview
authors: Bureau of Justice Assistance, Office of Justice Programs
sources.summary: BJA overview of federal support for adult treatment courts. Notes DOJ has supported treatment courts for decades; programs integrate evidence-based substance-use treatment, testing, sanctions and incentives, and recovery support under judicial supervision. Outcomes depend on program design and implementation.
key_findings: Federal justice agencies have long supported adult treatment-court models
Model elements include treatment, testing, sanctions/incentives, and recovery supports in supervised court settings
sources.limitations: Program overview, not a meta-analysis guaranteeing uniform recidivism reductions; quality varies by local design.
sources.notes: Supports Path C (addiction-driven conduct) as an evidence-informed option, not a universal mandate.

sources.title: Mental health courts
authors: Bureau of Justice Assistance, Office of Justice Programs
sources.summary: BJA taxonomy/resource hub recognizing mental health courts and related justice–behavioral-health collaboration for people with mental illness or co-occurring substance-use disorders.
key_findings: Federal justice programming recognizes specialized mental-health court and collaboration models
Behavioral-health and justice systems are treated as linked for relevant populations
sources.limitations: Taxonomy/resource page, not a single outcome study; does not prescribe a specific Community Safety Corps staffing model.
sources.notes: Supports Path D (mental-health crisis) collaboration framing.

sources.title: Recidivism
sources.summary: NIJ topic page on recidivism as a core justice-system measure. Emphasizes that measurement choices matter; rearrest, reconviction, and reincarceration capture different outcomes.
key_findings: Recidivism is a fundamental corrections/justice measure
Definition and measurement (rearrest vs reconviction vs reincarceration) affect interpretation
sources.limitations: Topic overview, not a single national rate claim; do not invent national recidivism percentages from this page alone.
sources.notes: Supports careful recidivism reporting for restoration campuses.

sources.title: Five Things About Reentry
sources.summary: NIJ brief describing reentry as a continuum from intake assessment and in-custody programming through release planning, supervision, and community reintegration. Stresses individualized, holistic supports and nuanced success measures beyond rearrest alone.
key_findings: Reentry is a continuum beginning during confinement, not only at the gate
Programs and services should be tailored; holistic supports matter
Success metrics should be more nuanced than rearrest alone
sources.limitations: Research synthesis brief; does not guarantee that any particular local reentry package will succeed.
sources.notes: Supports reentry-from-day-one doctrine without overclaiming outcomes.

sources.title: Impact of Prison Reentry Services on Short-Term Outcomes: Evidence From a Multisite Evaluation
sources.summary: NIJ-hosted multisite evaluation evidence on short-term outcomes of prison reentry services. Findings are mixed/modest in areas often including employment, housing, service access, and substance use rather than magical uniform success — supporting rigorous evaluation rather than blanket claims that every reentry service works.
key_findings: Reentry-service effects on short-term outcomes are not uniformly large
Supports cautious, evaluation-driven reentry policy
sources.limitations: Study vintage and sites limit generalizability; short-term outcomes are not lifetime success; read full report before citing specific effect sizes.
sources.notes: Use as evidence caution against overclaiming reentry program effectiveness.

sources.title: What Is Risk Assessment
authors: Bureau of Justice Assistance, Public Safety Risk Assessment Clearinghouse
sources.summary: BJA/PSRAC overview explaining actuarial risk assessment across justice stages. Risk scores are probabilistic, not definitive predictions; tools vary in validity; static vs dynamic factors matter; reassessment is important as circumstances change. Supports using validated tools to structure decisions and allocate resources — not as sole grounds for permanent custody.
key_findings: Risk assessments provide probabilistic, not certain, predictions of reoffending
Tool accuracy and validity can vary; tools should fit the population of use
Risk assessment can improve consistency and resource targeting when properly used
sources.limitations: Guidance overview, not a validation study of any particular tool; does not authorize score-only permanent confinement decisions.
sources.notes: Supports Permanent Public Safety System rule that a risk score alone is never enough.

sources.title: Amdt8.4.7 Conditions of Confinement
sources.summary: Constitution Annotated essay on Eighth Amendment conditions of confinement. Full essay retrieval was blocked by site security at registration time; the Annotated’s conditions-of-confinement materials are the intended legal map for the rule that confinement conditions cannot become cruel or deliberately indifferent to serious human needs. Detailed holdings require legal review and primary case citation before policy drafting.
key_findings: Eighth Amendment doctrine addresses conditions of confinement
Constitutional floor for humane custody remains binding regardless of sentence length
sources.limitations: Secondary annotation; retrieval blocked by Cloudflare at registration; do not invent specific case holdings from this registry entry alone — legal review required.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Congressional Research Service / Constitution Annotated institutional product.
sources.notes: Anchor for Secure Public Safety Campus constitutional-conditions note pending legal-review package.

sources.title: Bureau of Prisons: Better Planning Could Help BOP Evaluate Its Care for Aging Inmates and Health Care Cost Control (GAO-17-379 context) / Better Planning and Evaluation Needed
sources.summary: GAO review of BOP inmate health-care costs FY2009–2016. Health-care obligations rose substantially; BOP cited an aging inmate population, rising pharmaceutical prices, and increasing costs of outside medical services among cost drivers. Supports the cost rationale for medical/geriatric custody planning — not a claim that every older person should be released.
key_findings: BOP health-care obligations rose from about $978 million (FY2009) to about $1.34 billion (FY2016)
BOP cited aging inmate population among factors affecting health-care costs
sources.limitations: Federal BOP health-care cost study; does not itself establish misconduct/rearrest differentials by age (see CC-SRC-028).
sources.notes: Use for aging-cost / resource-concentration design notes; do not invent state-system cost figures from this alone.

sources.title: The Impact of an Aging Inmate Population on the Federal Bureau of Prisons
authors: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Inspector General
sources.summary: DOJ OIG report on aging federal inmates. Finds aging inmates commit less misconduct while incarcerated and have lower post-release re-arrest rates in OIG sampling than the general federal inmate re-arrest rate cited from BOP research; also discusses limited early-release pathways and cost implications. Supports medical/geriatric secure-care and step-down consideration — not automatic release.
key_findings: Aging inmates represented a smaller share of misconduct incidents than their share of the population in the OIG analysis year
OIG sampling found lower re-arrest among aging releasees than the BOP general federal re-arrest rate referenced in the report
sources.limitations: Federal BOP context; sampling and comparison methods are report-specific; age reduces average risk but does not eliminate individual dangerousness; do not invent national percentages beyond careful quotation in later modules.
sources.notes: Corrects informal attribution of lower misconduct/rearrest solely to GAO-17-379; OIG 15-05 is the better federal source for that finding.

sources.title: First Step Act, Frequently Asked Questions
sources.summary: BOP FAQ summarizing First Step Act features relevant to resource concentration: expanded recidivism-reduction programming, earned time credits for eligible individuals, residential reentry/home-confinement opportunities, compassionate release / reduction-in-sentence pathways, and elderly-offender pilot mechanisms. Illustrates that federal law already contains tools to move eligible people out of expensive custody — without claiming all state systems match federal design.
key_findings: FSA expands risk-reduction programming and productive activities with earned time credits for eligible inmates
Compassionate release and elderly-offender/home-confinement mechanisms exist under federal practice described by BOP
sources.limitations: Federal BOP FAQ; eligibility exclusions apply; not an outcome evaluation; state systems differ.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: BOP operational FAQ interpreting statutory/program features.
sources.notes: Supports resource-concentration framing for Permanent Public Safety System affordability.

sources.title: Scope 1 and Scope 2 Inventory Guidance
authors: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Center for Corporate Climate Leadership
sources.summary: EPA guidance distinguishing Scope 1 direct GHG emissions from sources controlled or owned by an organization from Scope 2 indirect emissions associated with purchased electricity, steam, heat, or cooling. Supports requiring major projects to disclose and price both rather than appearing clean because emissions occur at a distant power plant.
key_findings: Scope 1 covers direct emissions from owned/controlled sources
Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heat, or cooling
sources.limitations: Inventory guidance for organizational GHG accounting, not a Constitutional Capitalism pricing statute; Scope 3 and local non-GHG burdens require separate modules.
sources.notes: Anchors total-footprint disclosure for Community Resource Compacts.

sources.title: Departments of the Interior, Agriculture Advance Mining Reforms Aimed at Protecting and Empowering Tribal Communities
sources.summary: Interior/Agriculture announcement of regulatory and policy recommendations to protect Tribal interests and resources from mining impacts, increase Tribal engagement in mining proposals, and promote well-designed mining that accounts for climate change and current standards and technologies. Directs earlier notice, consultation, reclamation/financial-assurance engagement, and related steps.
key_findings: Federal agencies framed mining expansion as requiring Tribal protection, engagement, and modern environmental/social standards
Recommendations include earlier Tribal notice, consultation on reclamation and financial assurance, and NEPA cooperating-agency efforts
sources.limitations: Press release and agency directives, not a complete national mining code; administration policy can change; does not invent state royalty or cleanup-bond statistics.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Biden-administration DOI/USDA announcement; later administrations may revise posture.
sources.notes: Supports mineral-compact consultation and responsibility framing without overclaiming permanence of specific federal reforms.

sources.title: EPA Unveils Clean Air Act-Related Resource to Provide Transparency for Data Center Developers, Local Communities, Tribes
sources.summary: EPA announcement of a Clean Air Act Resources for Data Centers webpage covering regulatory information for power sources and backup generation (including stationary combustion turbines and engines), air permitting resources, and modeling guidance. Confirms federal recognition that data-center power and backup generation raise air-quality and permitting issues for developers, communities, and Tribes.
key_findings: EPA created dedicated CAA resources for data-center and AI facility development
Power sources and backup generation are highlighted as major planning/permitting concerns
sources.limitations: CAA-focused transparency/permitting resource, not an endorsement of any specific Community Resource Compact pricing design; administration framing emphasizes accelerated development.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: EPA under Trump administration framing AI/data-center acceleration alongside cooperative federalism.
sources.notes: Supports distinct data-center compact disclosure of backup-generation and air-quality implications.

sources.title: Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP)
sources.summary: EPA Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program requires reporting from large GHG emission sources, fuel and industrial gas suppliers, and CO2 injection sites; data are made public. As of registration, EPA had also proposed reconsideration that would permanently remove program obligations for many source categories — illustrating that federal reporting rules are politically changeable and should not be treated as a durable Constitutional Capitalism floor.
key_findings: Large facilities report facility-level GHG information under GHGRP when covered
Federal reporting obligations can be expanded or reduced by later rulemaking
sources.limitations: Coverage, thresholds, and continuity are rule-dependent; proposed reconsideration (noted on EPA page) underscores instability; not a complete pollution ledger for water, toxics, noise, or land use.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Federal regulatory program subject to administration change.
sources.notes: Supports Resource and Pollution Ledger as a durable public design beyond any single federal reporting regime.

sources.title: NRCS Climate-Smart Mitigation Activities
sources.summary: NRCS page on climate-smart mitigation activities recognizing conservation practices — including soil-management systems such as cover crops, conservation tillage, agroforestry, compost, biochar, and related tools — as potential climate-mitigation and co-benefit practices for soil health, water quality, erosion, and habitat.
key_findings: USDA/NRCS frames specific conservation practices as climate-smart mitigation activities
Practices are associated with soil, water, erosion, and habitat co-benefits in agency framing
sources.limitations: Program/practice catalog, not a verification protocol for a Local Carbon Restoration Exchange; outcomes vary by soil, climate, and management; do not invent sequestration rates.
sources.notes: Supports regenerative-farm payment examples; measurement credibility still required (see CC-SRC-035).

sources.title: USDA Launches First Phase of Soil Carbon Monitoring Efforts through Conservation Reserve Program Initiative
sources.summary: USDA/FSA announcement of a $10 million initiative to sample, measure, and monitor soil carbon on Conservation Reserve Program acres to better quantify climate outcomes, with university and partner projects for grasses, trees, and wetlands. Demonstrates why credible measurement and monitoring must be central to any local carbon-restoration payment system.
key_findings: USDA invested in soil-carbon sampling/monitoring on CRP acres
Agency framing ties measurement to improved modeling and conservation planning
sources.limitations: CRP-focused initiative; not a national mandatory soil-carbon market; measurement science continues to evolve; do not invent carbon-credit prices or permanence guarantees.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: USDA climate-mitigation framing under the announcing administration.
sources.notes: Supports anti-fraud measurement requirements for Local Carbon Restoration Exchange.

sources.title: Community Solar Basics
sources.summary: DOE defines community solar as any solar project or purchasing program, within a geographic area, in which the benefits flow to multiple customers such as individuals, businesses, nonprofits, and other groups. Notes bill credits, access for renters and households unable to host rooftop solar, and related consumer-protection considerations.
key_findings: Community solar benefits flow to multiple customers within a geographic area
Can expand solar access beyond rooftop-capable households
sources.limitations: Community-solar definition page; community microgrids and other generation types require separate DOE/program modules and should not be over-attributed to this page alone.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: DOE Solar Energy Technologies Office / CMEI framing.
sources.notes: Supports community-owned energy design agenda; microgrids listed as options without claiming this page defines them.

sources.title: Food Security in the U.S.
sources.summary: ERS topic hub defining food security as access by all people at all times to enough food for an active, healthy life. Leads federal research and measurement on household and community food security; also points to Food Access Research Atlas and Food Environment Atlas tools.
key_findings: USDA ERS defines food security as access by all people at all times to enough food for an active, healthy life
ERS maintains research and measurement programs for U.S. household food security
sources.limitations: Definition and research hub, not a local production-capacity statute; do not invent food-insecurity percentages from this architecture slice.
sources.notes: Anchors food-as-infrastructure doctrine in the federal access definition while extending to place-based capacity.

sources.title: Wasted Food Scale
sources.summary: EPA Wasted Food Scale (update to the earlier Food Recovery Hierarchy) prioritizes pathways that prevent wasted food, donate, and upcycle before less preferred disposal pathways. Emphasizes that wasting food wastes the resources used to produce it; donation keeps food for its intended purpose of nourishing people.
key_findings: Preventing wasted food is the most preferred pathway
Donation and upcycling are preferred over landfill, incineration, and drain disposal
sources.limitations: Environmental ranking of management pathways; does not alone set economic/social design for a State Food Exchange; scale notes it does not consider economic and social factors.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: EPA sustainable management of food framing.
sources.notes: Supports surplus-to-people/reserves design without inventing national waste rates as locked doctrine claims.

sources.title: Local Agriculture Market Program (LAMP)
sources.summary: USDA AMS Local Agriculture Market Program supports development, coordination, and expansion of direct producer-to-consumer marketing; local and regional food markets and enterprises; and value-added agricultural products. Goals include regional food economies, value-added production strategies, mid-tier value chains, and producer income/opportunity.
key_findings: Federal program family explicitly supports local/regional markets and value-added agricultural products
Program goals include connecting regional food economies and strengthening mid-tier value chains
sources.limitations: Grant/program umbrella, not evidence that any specific State Food Exchange design works; outcomes vary by project.
sources.notes: Supports Regional Food Network, value-local, and local/regional market infrastructure design agendas.

sources.title: Local Food Research and Development
authors: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, Local and Regional Foods Division
sources.summary: AMS Local and Regional Foods Division page describing purpose-driven research and tools supporting farmers and food businesses in local and regional markets — market access, finance bottlenecks, and scale-appropriate tools. Useful as institutional context for Community Food Dashboard measurement design.
key_findings: USDA AMS maintains a dedicated local/regional foods research and development function
Agency framing emphasizes actionable insights for farmers accessing high-value domestic markets
sources.limitations: Program overview, not a sourced baseline of local-food share for any state or county.
sources.notes: Supports dashboard/research agenda posture without inventing local-sourcing metrics.

sources.title: The Food and Nutrition Assistance Landscape: Fiscal Year 2024 Annual Report (EIB-291)
sources.summary: ERS annual landscape report. FY2024 SNAP spending $99.8 billion; average monthly participation 41.7 million people; participation rate 12.3 percent. Notes 1% participation decline from FY2023 and expiration of emergency allotments contributing to spending decline.
key_findings: FY2024 SNAP average monthly participation: 41.7 million
FY2024 SNAP participation rate: 12.3%
FY2024 SNAP federal spending: $99.8 billion
sources.limitations: National program statistics; does not alone prescribe Constitutional Capitalism assistance redesign.
sources.notes: Primary source for SNAP scale context in Assistance Doctrine; do not treat caseload as permanent work-disconnection.

sources.title: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) — Key Statistics and Research
sources.summary: ERS SNAP key statistics page. SNAP is not targeted to a single subgroup. FY2023 household characteristics: 28% of SNAP households had earned income; among households with children, 55% had earned income; adults 18–59 were 42% of participants, children about 39%, adults 60+ about 19%. Points to Landscape FY2024 report for recent participation totals.
key_findings: SNAP households are diverse and include workers, children, and older adults
In FY2023, 28% of SNAP households had earned income; 55% of households with children had earned income
sources.limitations: Composition figures cited are FY2023 Characteristics series context on the page; FY2024 totals come from Landscape EIB-291.
sources.notes: Supports claim that SNAP caseload ≠ permanently disconnected from work.

sources.title: Effective Marginal Tax Rates / Benefit Cliffs
authors: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, ASPE
sources.summary: ASPE series on effective marginal tax rates and benefit cliffs — situations where lost benefits equal or exceed the earnings increase that triggered the reduction — and how phaseouts affect workers.
key_findings: Benefit cliffs occur when lost benefits equal or exceed the earnings increase that triggered the reduction
Benefit phaseouts contribute to effective marginal tax rates facing workers
sources.limitations: Federal research framing and tools; does not set a specific Constitutional Capitalism phaseout rate.
sources.notes: Supports benefit-cliff architecture; exact CC phaseout rates require modeling.

sources.title: Lessons Learned Deploying a Marginal Tax Rate Calculator
authors: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, ASPE
sources.summary: ASPE lessons from deploying a calculator designed to help people with low incomes predict how earnings changes affect benefits and effective marginal tax rates.
key_findings: Benefit-impact calculators can help workers anticipate how earnings changes affect assistance
Deployment lessons inform transparency and navigator design
sources.limitations: Tooling/lessons report; not evidence that any specific national calculator design is complete.
sources.notes: Supports universal calculator design agenda inside Human Prosperity Account.

sources.title: Work Requirements and Work Supports for Recipients of Means-Tested Benefits
sources.summary: CBO analysis of work requirements and work supports for recipients of means-tested benefits. Effects vary and can be uncertain; requirements may increase employment for some people while reducing benefits and income for others.
key_findings: Effects of work requirements and work supports vary and can be uncertain
Requirements may increase employment for some while reducing benefits and income for others
sources.limitations: Federal budget/research synthesis; not a prescription for any single state design.
sources.notes: Supports pairing requirements with genuine supports and independent evaluation.

sources.title: Understanding Economic Risk for Low-Income Families
authors: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, ASPE
sources.summary: ASPE research on economic risk for low-income families, including administrative burden pathways such as repeated reapplication, job instability, and benefit loss as sources of risk.
key_findings: Administrative burden and benefit instability contribute to economic risk for low-income households
Repeated reapplication, job instability, and benefit loss are identified risk sources
sources.limitations: Risk framing research; does not alone quantify Constitutional Capitalism fraud-control designs.
sources.notes: Supports fraud-without-humiliation and burden-reduction architecture.

sources.title: The Court and Constitutional Interpretation
authors: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.summary: Official Supreme Court page on constitutional interpretation. States that judicial review is not explicitly provided in the Constitution, was anticipated by Founders, and was confirmed in Marbury v. Madison (1803). Describes the Court as invalidating legislation or executive actions conflicting with the Constitution and notes that constitutional rulings are virtually final absent amendment or a new Court ruling.
key_findings: Judicial review function not explicitly provided in the Constitution
Power confirmed in Marbury v. Madison (1803)
Court may invalidate legislation or executive actions conflicting with the Constitution
sources.limitations: Institutional self-description; not a statute and not an exhaustive history of judicial review debates.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Issued by the Court whose role is described.
sources.notes: Baseline for People’s Branch / judicial-review design; does not alone prescribe reform.

sources.title: Code of Conduct for Justices of the Supreme Court of the United States
authors: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.summary: First formal Code of Conduct for Supreme Court Justices, issued November 13, 2023, addressing ethics expectations for Justices.
key_findings: Formal Code of Conduct for Justices issued November 2023
Addresses ethics expectations for Supreme Court Justices
sources.limitations: Code content and enforcement mechanisms are distinct questions; presence of a code does not alone establish independent external enforcement.
sources.notes: Supports claim that a formal code now exists; CC proposes stronger enforceable external review.

sources.title: Statement of the Court Regarding the Code of Conduct (accompanying materials)
authors: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.summary: Court statement accompanying the November 2023 Code of Conduct for Justices.
key_findings: Court publicly issued a formal ethics code for Justices in November 2023
sources.limitations: Same PDF family as CC-SRC-048; listed to preserve citation trail from design brief.
sources.notes: Paired with CC-SRC-048.

sources.title: Initiative and Referendum Overview and Resources
sources.summary: NCSL overview of statewide initiative and referendum. States that 24 states have an initiative process enabling citizens to place statutes and, in some states, constitutional amendments on the ballot; also discusses popular referendum.
key_findings: 24 states have a statewide initiative process per NCSL
First state initiative adoption: South Dakota 1898; most recent Mississippi 1992 per NCSL overview
sources.limitations: Counts and classifications can change; distinguish initiative-only from initiative-or-referendum totals used by other trackers.
sources.notes: Direct fetch was intermittently blocked by bot protection; count confirmed via NCSL page excerpt in search results and aligned with design brief.

sources.title: Recall of State Officials
sources.summary: NCSL report on state recall. Key takeaway: nineteen states allow recall of state officials; processes vary; federal officials are outside this state-recall framework.
key_findings: 19 states allow recall elections of state officials
Virginia has a petition-triggered recall trial rather than a recall election and is not counted among the 19
sources.limitations: State-level only; does not create federal recall authority.
sources.notes: Supports descriptive recall baseline for People’s Branch design.

sources.title: ArtV.3.3 Proposals of Amendments by Convention — Constitution Annotated
sources.summary: Constitution Annotated essay on Article V proposals of amendments by convention, within the broader Article V structure of congressional proposal or convention on state applications and state ratification — without a direct national citizen-petition amendment route.
key_findings: Article V contemplates proposal by Congress or by convention after state applications
No direct national citizen-petition pathway in Article V text as annotated
sources.limitations: Annotation is interpretive; ratification mechanics detailed across related essays.
sources.notes: URL from design brief; fetch timed out in session — treat as registered official annotation target; claim wording kept conservative.

sources.title: Good Behavior Clause Doctrine — Constitution Annotated
sources.summary: Constitution Annotated essay on the Good Behavior Clause doctrine for federal judges, supporting the conventional understanding that Article III judges serve during good behavior (life tenure absent removal), which is why durable fixed active Supreme Court terms are treated as likely requiring amendment.
key_findings: Good Behavior Clause is the textual anchor for federal judicial tenure during good behavior
sources.limitations: Doctrine essays summarize contested interpretive history; legal drafting for term limits remains separate.
sources.notes: URL from design brief; fetch timed out — conservative claim wording.

sources.title: ArtII.S4.4.10 Judicial Impeachments — Constitution Annotated
sources.summary: Constitution Annotated essay on judicial impeachments: federal judges are subject to impeachment and conviction framework rather than ordinary electoral recall.
key_findings: Federal judicial removal is framed through impeachment practice and standards
sources.limitations: Historical impeachment practice is sparse; does not itself design a Judicial Accountability Council.
sources.notes: Supports current-law baseline that ordinary voter recall of federal judges is not the constitutional removal path.

sources.title: Citizen Initiative Subject Rules
sources.summary: NCSL overview of subject restrictions on citizen initiatives (single-subject and related boundaries), illustrating that initiative systems commonly need carefully defined boundaries.
key_findings: Some initiative states restrict subjects, appropriations, or court-related measures
sources.limitations: State rules vary; does not prescribe CC anti-wealth financing rules.
sources.notes: Supports need for initiative boundaries and safeguards.

sources.title: U.S. primary energy production, consumption, and exports increased in 2024
sources.summary: EIA Today in Energy: United States continued to produce more energy than it consumed in 2024; energy exports grew to a record 30.9 quads; net exports of 9.3 quads were the highest in EIA records dating to 1949.
key_findings: U.S. produced more primary energy than it consumed in 2024
Record energy exports 30.9 quads in 2024
Net energy exports 9.3 quads — highest in EIA records since 1949
sources.limitations: Primary-energy accounting; does not measure public vs private capture of export value.
sources.notes: Fetched page body 2026-08-05.

sources.title: U.S. electricity generation in 2025 hit a record, again
sources.summary: EIA Today in Energy: U.S. electricity net generation reached a record 4.43 thousand terawatthours in 2025, up 2.8% from 2024.
key_findings: Record U.S. electricity net generation 4.43 thousand TWh in 2025
sources.limitations: Generation total is not by itself a reliability or affordability measure.
sources.notes: Fetched page body 2026-08-05.

sources.title: U.S. crude oil production rose in 2025, setting new record
sources.summary: EIA Today in Energy / STEO-based article: U.S. crude oil production set a new annual record of 13.6 million barrels per day in 2025 (about 3% / 350,000 b/d above prior year).
key_findings: Record U.S. crude oil production 13.6 million b/d in 2025
sources.limitations: STEO-linked annual estimate; revisions possible as monthly series finalize.
sources.notes: EIA page title and key figure confirmed via official EIA search excerpt 2026-08-05.

sources.title: Natural Gas Imports and Exports Monthly — December 2025
sources.summary: DOE monthly report: YTD 2025 LNG exports by vessel 5,506.9 Bcf (~5.5 Tcf), up 26% from YTD 2024 4,365.4 Bcf — supporting a record ~5.5 Tcf annual LNG export level.
key_findings: YTD 2025 LNG by vessel exports 5,506.9 Bcf (~5.5 Tcf)
About 26% increase versus YTD 2024
sources.limitations: DOE monthly series; EIA Natural Gas Monthly may revise; do not treat as proof of public-return institutions.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Official federal energy department statistical publication.
sources.notes: PDF fetched 2026-08-05; used for LNG annual total cited in Energy Sovereignty brief.

sources.title: Oil and petroleum products explained — Oil imports and exports
sources.summary: EIA Energy Explained: United States became a total petroleum net exporter in 2020; even while net exporting, the United States still imported some crude oil and petroleum products for domestic demand and international markets; remained a net crude oil importer in 2022 in the page’s cited year.
key_findings: U.S. became total petroleum net exporter in 2020
Net exporter status coexists with continued crude/product imports
sources.limitations: Page examples use 2022 figures; update as EIA refreshes; supports sovereignty-not-autarky framing, not fund design.
sources.notes: Fetched page body 2026-08-05.

sources.title: Ten years after first Sabine Pass cargo, U.S. LNG exports are still on the rise
sources.summary: EIA Today in Energy: U.S. is the world’s largest LNG exporter; LNG exports rose from 0.5 Bcf/d in 2016 to 15.0 Bcf/d in 2025; February STEO forecasts exports exceeding 18.1 Bcf/d in 2027.
key_findings: U.S. LNG exports 15.0 Bcf/d in 2025
STEO forecast LNG exports exceed 18.1 Bcf/d in 2027
sources.limitations: Forecasts are uncertain; capacity expansions may slip.
sources.notes: Supports continued LNG export growth context; not a claim that exports automatically create public prosperity.

sources.title: CMS' Value-Based Programs
sources.summary: CMS describes value-based programs that reward health care providers with incentive payments for the quality of care they give to people with Medicare, as part of reforming how care is delivered and paid for.
key_findings: Value-based programs reward quality of care for Medicare beneficiaries with incentive payments
Programs are part of CMS quality strategy to reform delivery and payment
sources.limitations: Does not by itself quantify how complete the national transition from volume-based payment is.
sources.notes: Supports incomplete transition context; not proof that Constitutional Health System institutions exist.

sources.title: Rural Hospital Programs
sources.summary: HRSA rural hospital programs page states that between 2010 and 2025, 152 rural hospitals closed, of which 52 were Critical Access Hospitals.
key_findings: 152 rural hospitals closed between 2010 and 2025
52 of those closures were Critical Access Hospitals
sources.limitations: Closure definitions and inclusion of conversions can differ across trackers (e.g., Chartis reports higher totals).
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Official federal rural health agency page.
sources.notes: Direct fetch blocked from this environment; wording confirmed via search excerpt of HRSA page.

sources.title: Fast Facts: Health and Economic Costs of Chronic Conditions
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.summary: CDC states that ninety percent of the nation’s $5.3 trillion in annual health care expenditures are for people with chronic and mental health conditions.
key_findings: 90% of $5.3T annual health care expenditures are for people with chronic and mental health conditions
sources.limitations: Wording covers spending for people who have those conditions — not that 90% of spending is solely treatment of those conditions.
sources.notes: Page is JS-rendered; wording confirmed via search excerpt. Do not paraphrase as ‘90% treats chronic disease.’

sources.title: Report Assesses Access to Primary Care in Arkansas
sources.summary: ACHI summarizes Milbank Memorial Fund findings: 18% of Arkansas adults report not having a usual source of care (nearly 1 in 5), comparable to a national estimate of 17%.
key_findings: 18% of Arkansas adults report not having a usual source of care
Nearly 1 in 5 Arkansans lack a usual source of care
National estimate cited as 17%
sources.limitations: Secondary summary of Milbank report; definitions of usual source of care are survey-based.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Arkansas Center for Health Improvement policy communication.
sources.notes: Supports Arkansas primary-care access diagnosis; not proof of CC institutions.

sources.title: Critical Access Hospitals
sources.summary: CMS describes Critical Access Hospitals as a separate Medicare provider type with distinct Conditions of Participation and payment method, and links Rural Emergency Hospitals as a related rural facility model.
key_findings: CAHs are a separate Medicare provider type with distinct CoPs and payment method
CMS maintains a Rural Emergency Hospitals certification pathway alongside CAHs
sources.limitations: Describes existing federal models; does not establish a complete Community Health Readiness Budget system.
sources.notes: Supports descriptive baseline that distinct rural payment models already exist.

sources.title: Student Loan Repayment & Scholarship Programs
sources.summary: ADH Primary Care Office page on student loan repayment and scholarship programs notes HRSA and VA initiatives that reduce financial barriers for health professionals while addressing workforce shortages in underserved communities.
key_findings: ADH publishes loan repayment and scholarship program information for healthcare workforce
Programs aim to reduce financial barriers and improve access in underserved communities
sources.limitations: Program catalog page; does not quantify Arkansas placement outcomes for this claim.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Official Arkansas Department of Health page.
sources.notes: Supports existing pipeline fragments; CC proposes coordination into a full rural academy pipeline.

sources.title: Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA) Information
sources.summary: SSA COLA information: Social Security and SSI benefits for 75 million Americans increase 2.8% in 2026; nearly 71 million Social Security beneficiaries see the COLA beginning January 2026; nearly 7.5 million SSI recipients begin December 31, 2025.
key_findings: Nearly 71 million Social Security beneficiaries receive the 2026 COLA beginning January 2026
2.8 percent COLA for 2026
sources.limitations: Beneficiary counts are point-in-time program announcements and can change with enrollment.
sources.notes: Direct /cola/ path blocked in this environment; wording confirmed via SSA news COLA page search excerpt and press release.

sources.title: Trustees Report Summary
sources.summary: 2026 Trustees Report Summary: OASI Trust Fund can pay 100% of scheduled benefits until the fourth quarter of 2032; thereafter continuing income sufficient to pay 78% of scheduled benefits under intermediate assumptions unless Congress acts.
key_findings: OASI reserves projected depleted Q4 2032
About 78% of scheduled OASI benefits payable thereafter from continuing income
sources.limitations: Intermediate assumptions; projections revise annually; combined OASDI depletion timing differs from OASI-alone.
sources.notes: Use OASI-specific 2032/78% wording carefully; do not confuse with combined OASDI 2034/83%.

sources.title: Older Workers: Retirement Account Disparities Have Increased by Income and Persisted by Race Over Time
sources.summary: GAO analysis of SCF data on households ages 51–64: about one in ten low-income households had a retirement account balance in 2019 (down from about one in five in 2007), while about nine in ten high-income households had a balance through the period.
key_findings: About 1 in 10 low-income near-retirement households had a retirement account balance in 2019
About 9 in 10 high-income households had a balance 2007–2019
sources.limitations: Household survey; ages 51–64; income quintile definitions in report; not a claim about all ages.
sources.notes: Supports caution against converting Social Security entirely into defined-contribution accounts.

sources.title: Employee stock ownership plans (ESOPs)
sources.summary: IRS: an ESOP is an IRC 401(a) qualified defined contribution plan that is a stock bonus plan (or stock bonus/money purchase plan) and must be designed to invest primarily in qualifying employer securities.
key_findings: ESOPs are defined contribution plans designed to invest primarily in qualifying employer securities
sources.limitations: Describes ESOP legal design; does not evaluate diversification adequacy for national retirement policy.
sources.notes: Supports diversification-safeguard framing for Citizen Ownership Accounts beyond employer stock.

sources.title: Primary Insurance Amount
sources.summary: SSA OACT PIA formula page: for 2026 eligibility, PIA equals 90% of the first $1,286 of AIME, plus 32% of AIME between $1,286 and $7,749, plus 15% of AIME over $7,749 — a progressive bend-point structure.
key_findings: 2026 PIA bend points $1,286 and $7,749
Replacement factors 90%, 32%, and 15% across AIME segments
sources.limitations: Formula progressivity describes replacement of AIME segments; individual replacement rates vary with career earnings and claiming age.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Official SSA Office of the Chief Actuary page.
sources.notes: Use for progressive-replacement design claim separate from COLA beneficiary counts.

sources.title: America’s Farms and Ranches at a Glance: 2024 Edition
sources.summary: ERS EIB-283 using 2023 ARMS: family farms about 96% of farms and 83% of production value; small family farms about 86% of farms, 41% of land, 17% of production value; large-scale family farms about 48% of production value.
key_findings: Family farms ≈96% of farms and ≈83% of production value (2023)
Small family farms ≈86% of farms but ≈17% of production value
2023: midsize+large family farms ≈66% of production value and ≈71% of countercyclical-type payments
Small family farms received ≈76% of CRP payments (different program incidence)
sources.limitations: GCFI-based size classes; covers contiguous U.S. in ARMS methodology; not a claim that small farms lack importance.
sources.notes: Supports family-farm centrality and small-farm production-share context for prosperity doctrine. | Also used for agriculture influence dossier: payment incidence by farm size (not influence proof).

sources.title: 2023 Farm to School Census
sources.summary: FNS 2023 Farm to School Census (SY 2022–23): nearly 74% of SFAs reported at least one farm-to-school activity; participating SFAs spent almost $1.8 billion on local purchases, about 16% of total food spending; availability and cost remain common challenges.
key_findings: ≈74% of SFAs reported farm-to-school activity in SY 2022–23
≈$1.8B local purchases ≈16% of participating SFA food spending
sources.limitations: Local definitions vary; fluid milk is a large share of local spending; not a finished Constitutional Capitalism purchase-guarantee design.
sources.notes: Supports institutional local-purchase feasibility context; illustrative CC floors still require modeling.

sources.title: 2025 Investment Company Fact Book — Quick Facts Guide
sources.summary: ICI quick facts: U.S. retirement market about $44.1 trillion at year-end 2024; IRAs $17.0T and DC plans $12.4T were 67% of total; mutual funds managed 45% of those account-based retirement assets.
key_findings: US retirement market ≈$44.1T YE2024
IRAs + DC ≈67% of retirement market; mutual funds manage ≈45% of those account-based assets
sources.limitations: Industry association data; mutual-fund share does not by itself measure local vs global equity exposure inside funds.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: ICI represents investment companies; figures are widely cited market statistics.
sources.notes: Supports diagnosis that retirement savings are heavily pooled in national fund vehicles.

sources.title: Municipal Market Facts / Municipal Market Year in Review (MSRB; Fed Financial Accounts)
authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
sources.summary: MSRB materials summarizing Federal Reserve Financial Accounts holder data for municipal securities: large market financed as debt instruments; households and mutual funds are major holders receiving contractual bond returns rather than automatic resident project equity.
key_findings: Municipal capital is raised primarily through municipal securities markets
Households and funds are major holders of munis as debt claims (interest/principal), not resident equity upside by default
sources.limitations: Holder categories do not prove whether bondholders live in the issuing locality; supports structure of debt vs equity, not a claim that all returns leave town.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: MSRB is the municipal market self-regulatory organization; underlying holder data from Fed Financial Accounts.
sources.notes: Supports Community Investment Units as a design alternative/complement to debt-only capital raising.

sources.title: ISO Public Protection Classification (PPC) Program
authors: ISO / Verisk Community Hazard Mitigation Services
sources.summary: ISO PPC program classifies community fire-protection capability from Class 1 (generally superior) to Class 10 (does not meet minimum criteria) using the Fire Suppression Rating Schedule; program materials state that better classifications help secure lower fire insurance premiums and that insurers use PPC information in premium setting.
key_findings: PPC classes 1–10 rate community fire-protection capability
Program links better public fire protection to lower fire insurance premiums for communities
sources.limitations: Private rating schedule; premium effects vary by insurer and other underwriting factors; not a government standard.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Commercial risk-assessment product widely used in U.S. property insurance markets.
sources.notes: Supports insurance–fire-protection market link for Community Resilience doctrine.

sources.title: Volunteer Firefighter Crisis (NFPA Journal summary of NFPA research)
sources.summary: NFPA Journal article summarizing NFPA research: volunteer firefighter ranks fell from about 827,000 in 2008 to about 635,000 in 2023; fire department call volume rose about 70% over that period (roughly 25 million to 42 million).
key_findings: Volunteer firefighters ≈635,000 in 2023 vs ≈827,000 in 2008
Fire department calls ≈+70% since 2008
sources.limitations: Journal summary of underlying NFPA statistical series; department-type mix and EMS share of calls matter for interpretation.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: NFPA is a standards and research organization for fire protection.
sources.notes: Supports volunteer recruitment/retention pressure diagnosis for rural resilience pathways.

sources.title: Employee Ownership by the Numbers
sources.summary: NCEO analysis of DOL Form 5500 ESOP filings for plan year 2023: 6,609 ESOPs at 6,411 unique companies; about 15.1 million participants including about 11.0 million active; over $2 trillion in total plan assets; 309 new ESOPs reported in 2023.
key_findings: 6,609 ESOPs / 6,411 companies (plan year 2023)
~15.1M participants (~11.0M active); >$2T plan assets
sources.limitations: NCEO tabulation of DOL filings; public vs private ESOP participant mix differs; not a claim about all employee-ownership forms.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: NCEO promotes employee ownership research and education; figures drawn from official DOL filings.
sources.notes: Supports employee ownership as an established U.S. channel for Local Ownership doctrine.

sources.title: USDA Annual Survey of U.S. Agricultural Cooperatives (2024 results summary)
sources.summary: USDA annual survey: 1,620 farmer, rancher, and fishery cooperatives in 2024; cooperative revenues about $275.8 billion; net income before taxes about $11 billion; co-op count declined from 1,647 in 2023 mainly via mergers.
key_findings: 1,620 ag cooperatives in 2024
≈$275.8B cooperative revenues in 2024
sources.limitations: Covers agricultural co-ops, not all consumer/worker co-ops; count declines partly reflect mergers, not only dissolution.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Official USDA Rural Development cooperative statistics.
sources.notes: Supports member-owned cooperative enterprise as a major agricultural ownership channel.

sources.title: The State of Labor Market Competition
sources.summary: Treasury report (with DOJ/DOL/FTC consultation) on employer power in U.S. labor markets: concentration, frictions, and anti-competitive practices associated with wages and conditions below competitive benchmarks; policy recommendations included.
key_findings: Documents employer concentration and practices as sources of labor-market power
Estimates material wage effects from lack of competition relative to competitive benchmark (report synthesis; not a single local HHI estimate)
sources.limitations: Administration report synthesizing literature; effect-size figures are contested across studies; not Arkansas-specific; not a substitute for market-level identification.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Executive-branch policy report under competition agenda.
sources.notes: Supports CC-CLAIM-015 with qualification; also contrary-boundary for overclaiming national uniformity.

sources.title: Labor Market Monopsony: Trends, Consequences, and Policy Responses
sources.summary: CEA issue brief on labor-market monopsony: employer concentration and related practices can reduce wages relative to competitive settings; discusses trends and policy responses.
key_findings: Frames monopsony as distinct from product-market monopoly with shared causes
Links limited employer sets in local markets to wage-setting power
sources.limitations: 2016 brief; literature evolved; aging for current-state claims without refresh.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: White House CEA product (Obama administration archive).
sources.notes: Historical-by-design government synthesis for CC-CLAIM-015.

sources.title: Corporate Tax Incidence: A Review of Empirical Estimates and Analysis
sources.summary: CBO working paper reviewing empirical studies of corporate income tax incidence across countries and U.S. states; documents that labor may bear a portion of the burden under some estimates while methods and magnitudes are contested.
key_findings: Surveys cross-country and cross-state empirical approaches to wage effects of corporate taxes
Does not settle a single incidence share; emphasizes methodological limits
sources.limitations: 2011 review; subsequent agency assumptions evolved; not proof of consumer price incidence.
sources.notes: Best official review spine for CC-CLAIM-014.

sources.title: An Overview of the Corporate Income Tax System (CRS Report R47519)
sources.summary: CRS overview of the U.S. corporate income tax, including how CBO/JCT/Treasury allocate corporate-tax burden between capital and labor in distributional tables (illustratively capital majority / labor minority shares).
key_findings: Documents agency incidence assumptions used in distributional analysis (e.g., CBO/JCT capital-majority / labor-minority splits)
Notes evolution from earlier capital-only assumptions
sources.limitations: CRS synthesis of agency modeling assumptions — not an independent causal estimate; consumer price channel often excluded in agency tables.
sources.notes: Supports 'may be borne partly by workers' wording; does not prove consumer burden.

sources.title: Quarterly Retail E-Commerce Sales Report
sources.summary: Census quarterly estimates of U.S. retail e-commerce sales and share of total retail sales. Q1 2026 seasonally adjusted e-commerce share reported at 16.9% of total retail sales.
key_findings: Q1 2026 e-commerce ≈ 16.9% of total retail sales (seasonally adjusted)
Provides official time series for e-commerce penetration — not local leakage
sources.limitations: National retail sales concept; does not measure local wealth leakage, platform margins, or community multipliers.
sources.notes: Establishes e-commerce scale; NON-SUPPORTING for unquantified leakage claim as written.

sources.title: South Dakota v. Wayfair, Inc., 585 U.S. ___ (2018)
authors: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.summary: Supreme Court overruled physical-presence rule of Quill/Bellas Hess for state sales-tax collection, allowing states to require collection by remote sellers meeting economic nexus thresholds.
key_findings: Physical-presence rule for sales-tax collection overruled
Pre-Wayfair 'untaxed remote sales' narratives are legally outdated for collection authority
sources.limitations: Tax-collection nexus case — not an empirical local-leakage study.
sources.notes: Contrary/qualifier for obsolete fiscal narratives under CC-CLAIM-016.

sources.title: National Patterns of R&D Resources: 2023–24 Data Update (NSF 26-313)
authors: National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics, NSF
sources.summary: NCSES National Patterns integrates surveys of U.S. R&D funding and performance by sector (business, federal, higher education, nonprofit). Documents federal funding flowing to business and university performers among other patterns.
key_findings: Federal government funds R&D performed across sectors including businesses and universities
Provides official historical series for national R&D funding/performance
sources.limitations: Funding/performance accounts do not by themselves prove that specific private innovations would not have occurred without public funding.
sources.notes: Supports mild 'public research contributes to private innovation' with qualification.

sources.title: Labor Market Concentration
sources.summary: Peer-reviewed Journal of Human Resources study: labor-market concentration (HHI) across U.S. geographic-occupational markets associated with lower posted wages; average markets highly concentrated by DOJ-FTC thresholds.
key_findings: Average studied labor markets highly concentrated by merger-guideline thresholds
Higher concentration associated with lower posted wages (OLS/IV ranges reported)
sources.limitations: CareerBuilder vacancy data; identification debates; posted wages ≠ all compensation; not Arkansas-specific.
sources.notes: Peer-reviewed support for CC-CLAIM-015 conditional wording.

sources.title: Property Tax Relief for Homeowners
sources.summary: Lincoln Institute policy focus report on U.S. homeowner property-tax relief: documents affordability pressures and evaluates relief designs; notes property tax strengths while addressing overburden risks for some households.
key_findings: Property tax is central local revenue; some households face high burdens relative to income/liquidity
Targeted relief (e.g., circuit breakers, deferrals) preferred over blunt limits in authors' evaluation
sources.limitations: Institutional policy analysis — not proof that property tax generally threatens ownership security; state variation large; advocacy-adjacent institute.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Nonpartisan land-policy institute; policy recommendations present.
sources.notes: Qualifies CC-CLAIM-017; wording 'threaten ownership security' may overclaim — rewrite candidate.

sources.title: Productivity and Real Wages: Is There a Puzzle?
sources.summary: Brookings Papers discussion of productivity vs real wage measurement; illustrates how deflator and series choices alter apparent gaps — used here as contrary/measurement-dispute evidence for typical-worker gap narratives.
key_findings: Measurement and price-deflator choices materially affect productivity–wage comparisons
Historical scholarly challenge to treating a single gap series as unambiguous
sources.limitations: 1994 paper; historical by design for measurement debate; does not erase later BLS divergence documentation.
sources.notes: Contrary/measurement-dispute source for CC-CLAIM-002.

sources.title: Measuring labor market concentration using the QCEW
sources.summary: BLS Monthly Labor Review article measuring U.S. labor-market concentration with QCEW data (2002–2023). Finds average markets highly concentrated by DOJ/FTC guidelines and a significant negative association between employer concentration and wages; also simulates merger impacts on local labor-market power.
key_findings: Average U.S. labor market highly concentrated by 2010 DOJ/FTC guidelines in the study frame
Higher employer concentration significantly associated with lower wages in QCEW-based measures
sources.limitations: Association ≠ universal causal proof in every market; Arkansas transfer not automatic; merger simulations are counterfactual.
sources.notes: Closes CC-RQ-P21-014 dataset gap with official QCEW-based concentration measurement; supports CC-CLAIM-015 Qualifies.

sources.title: FEC Campaign Finance Data (disclosure portal)
sources.summary: Official FEC portal for federal campaign finance disclosures: candidate/committee receipts and disbursements, individual contributions, filings, and bulk data. Primary spine for lobbying/campaign-finance bibliography — does not by itself prove that economic concentration weakens democratic accountability.
key_findings: Federal campaign finance disclosures are publicly available for candidates and committees
Data enable research on money in politics but require careful identification for causal claims
sources.limitations: Disclosure ≠ capture. Does not measure lobbying influence or policy outcomes; state/local races largely outside FEC; OpenFEC API access separate.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Independent federal regulatory commission disclosure system.
sources.notes: Bibliography spine for CC-RQ-P21-025; NON-SUPPORTING for CC-CLAIM-003 as written.

sources.title: FEC Campaign Finance Statistics (summary tables)
sources.summary: FEC summary statistics tables for campaign financial activity by election cycle and filer type (candidates, parties, PACs, communications).
key_findings: Provides cycle-level summary tables for federal campaign finance activity
Useful for descriptive political-economy modules — not causal capture proofs
sources.limitations: Aggregate tables; causal inference requires research designs beyond the tables.
sources.notes: Companion to CC-SRC-092 for P0 bibliography closeout.

sources.title: Testing Theories of American Politics: Elites, Interest Groups, and Average Citizens
sources.summary: Peer-reviewed multivariate analysis of 1,779 U.S. policy issues arguing economic elites and organized business interests have substantial independent impacts on policy, while average citizens have little or no independent influence when preferences diverge — a key unequal-responsiveness result, not a proof of 'capture' or that economic concentration weakens democratic accountability as a single mechanism.
key_findings: Economic elites and business-oriented groups show independent association with policy outcomes in the study frame
Average citizens show little independent influence once elite/group preferences are controlled
sources.limitations: High preference correlation across income groups; causal identification debated; does not measure regulatory/state capture; not a campaign-contribution study; national-policy sample.
sources.notes: Best supporting literature for unequal policy responsiveness — PARTIAL adjacent to CC-CLAIM-003; NON-SUPPORTING for 'capture' synonymy.

sources.title: When Do the Rich Win?
sources.summary: Peer-reviewed Political Science Quarterly analysis of congruence when income groups disagree. Finds middle/rich/poor preferences usually align; when middle and rich disagree, the rich win only slightly more often — concluding the rich may matter more than they should but do not dominate policymaking. Direct contrary check on strong oligarchy/capture readings of Gilens/Page-type findings.
key_findings: Income groups almost always agree on policies in the analyzed cases
When middle and rich disagree, rich win only slightly more often; rich do not dominate
sources.limitations: Congruence design differs from Gilens/Page multivariate approach; does not settle all responsiveness debates.
sources.notes: Contrary evidence for strong capture/oligarchy claims linked to CC-CLAIM-003.

sources.title: Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA) Public Reports — LDA.gov
sources.summary: Official federal Lobbying Disclosure Act filings (LD-1 registrations, LD-2 quarterly activity, LD-203 contributions). Primary disclosure spine for lobbying activity — distinct from FEC campaign finance and from capture outcomes.
key_findings: Federal lobbying registrations and quarterly activity reports are publicly searchable/downloadable
Disclosure enables descriptive lobbying research; does not by itself prove capture
sources.limitations: Disclosure ≠ influence ≠ capture. Thresholds and reporting quality issues; state/local lobbying often outside LDA; does not measure policy outcomes.
sources.notes: Lobbying spine separate from FEC (CC-SRC-092/093) for CC-CLAIM-003 research.

sources.title: Effects of E-commerce on Local Labor Markets
sources.summary: IZA discussion paper exploiting state 'Amazon Tax' sales-tax collection mandates on out-of-state online retailers (2010–2016). Finds that removing the online price advantage lowers employment in transportation/warehousing complementary to e-commerce and produces net retail employment declines with brick-and-mortar losses partly offset by warehouse clubs/supercenters — evidence on local labor-market adjustment, not proof of 'wealth leakage' or platform extraction.
key_findings: Sales-tax collection mandates associated with lower transport/warehousing employment
Net local retail employment declines with within-retail reallocation
sources.limitations: Working paper; pre/post Amazon Tax design; not a community wealth-multiplier study; does not measure platform concentration or capital ownership leakage.
sources.notes: Supports local labor effects of e-commerce tax shocks — PARTIAL adjacent to CC-CLAIM-016; NON-SUPPORTING for 'wealth leakage' wording.

sources.title: Assessing the Gains from E-Commerce
sources.summary: AEJ: Macroeconomics study using Visa card transactions (2007–2017) estimating U.S. consumer surplus from e-commerce. Finds roughly 1% consumption-equivalent welfare gain by 2017 (>$1,000/household/year), mostly from access to merchants not available locally; higher-income and denser-county consumers gained more. Direct contrary/countervailing evidence against net-harm-only leakage narratives.
key_findings: Material consumer surplus from e-commerce variety/convenience
Gains larger for higher-income and denser counties in this U.S. sample
sources.limitations: Card-network sample; welfare to consumers ≠ local business/fiscal incidence; denser-county pattern complicates simple rural-access U.S. stories; does not measure community wealth leakage.
sources.notes: Contrary/countervailing consumer-welfare evidence for CC-CLAIM-016 net-harm framing.

sources.title: BEA Regional Input-Output Modeling System (RIMS II)
